description: From the 1933 boycott to Nuremberg Laws to Kristallnacht — persecution escalates to 1939.
content_html:
Nazi Racial Ideology and the Jews

At the heart of Nazi ideology was a virulent anti-Semitism. Hitler had argued in Mein Kampf that Jewish people were a separate and inferior race responsible for Germany’s defeat in 1918 and for the evils of communism and international capitalism. This was not merely personal hatred — it was a systematic ideology that divided humanity into a racial hierarchy with ‘Aryan’ Germans at the top and Jewish people at the bottom. This ideology shaped Nazi policy from the moment Hitler took power.

Before 1933, there were approximately 523,000 Jews in Germany, making up less than one percent of the population. They were a largely assimilated community — many were professionals, academics, lawyers, doctors and businesspeople who considered themselves German first. The persecution they faced after 1933 came not from popular demand, but was driven from above by the state, though it built on existing social prejudices that the Nazis deliberately inflamed.

Key Fact

The Nuremberg Laws (September 1935) stripped Jews of German citizenship and banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and non-Jews. They legally defined who was Jewish based on grandparentage, creating a bureaucratic framework for racial persecution.

Early Persecution: the 1933 Boycott

On 1 April 1933, the Nazi regime organised a national boycott of Jewish-owned businesses. SA stormtroopers stood outside Jewish shops, law offices and medical practices, intimidating customers and painting ‘Jude’ (Jew) on windows. The boycott lasted only one day because of international criticism and because many Germans did not observe it; but it signalled the regime’s intentions. Over the following months, Jews were expelled from the civil service under the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service (April 1933), removed from journalism, broadcasting and the arts, and excluded from many professions.

At the Nazi Party rally in Nuremberg in September 1935, Hitler announced two new laws that fundamentally altered the legal status of Jewish people in Germany. The Reich Citizenship Law stripped Jews of German citizenship, making them ‘subjects of the state’ rather than full citizens. The Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honour banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and non-Jews. Together, the Nuremberg Laws provided a legal framework for racial separation. Supplementary decrees defined who was ‘Jewish’ on the basis of grandparentage, creating categories of full Jews, half-Jews and quarter-Jews with different legal statuses.

Aryanisation and Economic Exclusion

Aryanisation was the forced transfer of Jewish-owned businesses into non-Jewish hands. Initially informal pressure and intimidation persuaded many Jewish business owners to sell cheaply; from 1937, the process became more systematic and legally enforced. Jewish professionals were progressively barred from their occupations. Jewish children were expelled from German schools. By late 1938, Jews had been almost entirely excluded from German economic life.

Key Fact

Kristallnacht (the Night of Broken Glass), 9–10 November 1938: approximately 7,500 Jewish businesses were smashed, around 267 synagogues were burned to the ground (and many more were damaged), at least 91 Jews were killed, and approximately 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps. The name refers to the broken glass that covered the streets.

On 7 November 1938, a young Jewish man, Herschel Grynszpan, shot a German diplomat in Paris, Ernst vom Rath, in protest at the deportation of his parents from Germany. When vom Rath died on 9 November, Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels used it as a pretext to orchestrate nationwide violence. SA and SS units, directed by the Nazi Party, attacked Jewish property across Germany. The violence was presented as a spontaneous popular reaction.

The aftermath was as devastating as the night itself. Jews were collectively fined one billion Reichsmarks for the damage done to their own property. Jewish emigration was officially encouraged — Jews were pressured to leave Germany but could only take a fraction of their assets. By September 1939, approximately half of Germany’s pre-1933 Jewish population had emigrated. The violence of Kristallnacht shocked international observers, though it produced no effective international response.

Historians describe the period 1933 to 1939 as one of escalating but not yet fully systematic persecution. The pattern was one of incremental radicalisation: each measure normalised the next. The 1933 boycott introduced public identification of Jews as targets; professional exclusions separated them from mainstream economic life; the Nuremberg Laws gave racial separation a legal framework; Aryanisation destroyed their economic independence; and Kristallnacht demonstrated that the state would use open violence with impunity. The international community’s muted reaction to Kristallnacht — expressions of horror but no sanctions, no military threat — was a signal that the regime noted. After September 1939, under the cover of war, persecution would escalate still further into systematic mass murder. Understanding the pre-war period is essential to understanding how that escalation became possible.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘Explain significance’ question on Kristallnacht, address both immediate significance (the violence, the fines, accelerated emigration) and longer-term significance (it marked a turning point — moving from legal discrimination to open physical violence; international community's muted response emboldened the regime; it showed that the state itself was directing anti-Jewish violence). For questions on the Nuremberg Laws, be precise: they stripped citizenship rights and banned marriage, and provided the bureaucratic framework for all subsequent racial legislation. Avoid describing the Nuremberg Laws as simply ‘making life hard for Jews’ — give the specific legal content.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Anti-Jewish persecution escalated in stages: the 1933 boycott and professional exclusions; the Nuremberg Laws (1935) stripping citizenship and banning intermarriage; Aryanisation of businesses from 1937.
  • Kristallnacht (9–10 November 1938) saw approximately 7,500 businesses smashed, around 267 synagogues burned to the ground (and many more damaged), and approximately 30,000 Jewish men arrested; Jews were then collectively fined for the damage.
  • By September 1939, approximately half of Germany’s pre-1933 Jewish population had emigrated under a combination of violence, legal exclusion and economic destruction of Jewish livelihoods.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Nuremberg Laws of 1935.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (2): identifies a specific feature with precise detail (e.g. the Reich Citizenship Law stripped Jews of German citizenship, making them subjects rather than citizens; the Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honour banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews). Secure (1–2): feature identified with some detail. Developing (1): vague reference to discrimination. Emerging (0–1): no relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Kristallnacht pogrom of November 1938.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each with precise detail — e.g. approximately 7,500 Jewish businesses smashed and windows broken (giving the event its name); approximately 30,000 Jewish men arrested and sent to concentration camps; around 267 synagogues burned to the ground (and many more damaged); Jews fined one billion Reichsmarks for the damage to their own property. Secure (3): two features with development. Developing (2): two features briefly stated. Emerging (1): one feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the escalation of anti-Jewish persecution in Germany between 1935 and 1938.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear cause (e.g. the regime used Aryanisation to seize Jewish economic assets from 1937, driven by desire for wealth transfer and ideological goals of removing Jews from economic life; OR: Herschel Grynszpan's shooting gave Goebbels a pretext for orchestrated violence) with specific evidence and link to escalation. Secure (3–4): cause identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Nuremberg Laws for the Jewish community in Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear consequence (e.g. Jews were made legally stateless — this gave state and local authorities the legal basis to exclude Jews from any area of life; the definition of 'Jewishness' by grandparentage trapped people who had not considered themselves Jewish; emigration became more attractive but assets could not be taken) with specific evidence and further effects. Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): vague mention.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Kristallnacht for the treatment of Jews in Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): significance at the time (open state-directed violence; mass arrests; billion-mark fine; immediate acceleration of emigration) AND over time (marked transition from legal discrimination to physical violence; international response inadequate, emboldening regime; precedent for further violence). Secure (5–6): both time periods. Developing (3–4): mainly descriptive. Emerging (1–2): brief mention without analysis.

practice_questions.text: 'The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 were the most significant turning point in the Nazi persecution of the Jews.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): agreement (Nuremberg Laws provided legal framework for all subsequent persecution; stripped citizenship; banned intermarriage; created bureaucratic definition of Jewishness) AND disagreement (Kristallnacht arguably more significant as turning point — shifted from legal discrimination to open violence; 1933 boycott and professional exclusions were the starting point; emigration pressure and Aryanisation also important). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both sides developed; judgement. Developing (4–6): one side stronger. Emerging (1–3): mainly descriptive.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the national boycott of Jewish businesses?

flashcard_questions.a: Two 1935 laws that stripped Jews of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews.
The forced transfer of Jewish-owned businesses to non-Jewish German owners, often at far below market value.
A Jewish man (Herschel Grynszpan) shot a German diplomat in Paris; Goebbels used this as a pretext.

flashcard_questions.q: Approximately how many Jewish businesses were smashed on Kristallnacht?
What financial penalty did Jews face after Kristallnacht?
flashcard_questions.a: A collective fine of one billion Reichsmarks for damage done to their own property.

flashcard_questions.q: Approximately how many of Germany's pre-1933 Jewish population had emigrated by September 1939?

flashcard_questions.a: Hostility and prejudice against Jewish people; a central feature of Nazi ideology.

flashcard_questions.q: What legal definition of 'Jewishness' did the Nuremberg Laws create?
flashcard_questions.a: Based on grandparentage — those with three or four Jewish grandparents were classified as full Jews.

glossary_terms.definition: Hostility and prejudice against Jewish people; a central component of Nazi ideology that drove state-sponsored persecution from 1933.
Two laws announced at the Nuremberg rally in September 1935 that stripped Jews of German citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews.
The process by which Jewish-owned businesses were forcibly transferred to non-Jewish (Aryan) German owners, often at far below market value, after 1933 and especially from 1937.
The forced emigration of Jews from Germany, accelerated after Kristallnacht, as the regime used violence and legal pressure to compel Jews to leave.

The Night of Broken Glass, 9–10 November 1938: a nationwide pogrom orchestrated by the Nazi Party in which approximately 7,500 Jewish businesses were smashed and around 267 synagogues were burned to the ground (and many more damaged).
The clause in the Treaty of Versailles that forced Germany to accept sole responsibility for the First World War, used to justify reparations and deeply resented by all Germans.
